source.title: Implicit ridge regularization provided by the minimum-norm least squares estimator when $n\ll p$
source.authors: D. Kobak; Jonathan Lomond; Benoit Sanchez

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether test risk can fall as an interpolating model gains dimensions, using linear regression rather than the ReLU networks in V2.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own results on minimum-norm least squares and test risk as dimensionality changes. It discusses neural-network findings from other work, but those cited findings are not rows here.
record.test_reason: The study measures prediction risk in linear and random-feature regression, not neural-network generalization as specified by any version. Its dimensionality sweeps resemble V2, but do not measure widening trained neural networks. The authors explicitly leave highly nonlinear models unexplained.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: minimum-norm least squares can generalize well when predictors greatly outnumber samples; low-variance predictors can supply implicit shrinkage, making positive ridge penalties unhelpful and sometimes making negative penalties preferable. The authors explicitly state that these results do not explain highly nonlinear underdetermined models such as deep neural networks.
record.recipe_differences: Studies underdetermined linear regression, spiked-covariance simulations, and random Fourier feature regression; does not use the neural-network training recipes in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Risk and the optimal ridge penalty vary with dimensionality and covariance structure; the paper reports different behavior for spherical and correlated predictors, and different risk curves across the MNIST training-set draws based on s²min.

fits_no_version.finding: Minimum-norm linear regression risk decreases beyond the interpolation threshold in the spiked-covariance simulation; adding suitably scaled random predictors also produces a post-interpolation decrease.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing predictor dimensionality can improve post-interpolation generalization in minimum-norm linear regression under suitable covariance and signal structure.

fits_no_version.finding: Positive ridge regularization loses its advantage in sufficiently high-dimensional correlated regression, and negative ridge penalties can improve prediction risk, including in the selected MNIST random-feature trials.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Implicit shrinkage in high-dimensional minimum-norm regression can make the optimal explicit ridge penalty zero or negative.

record.problems: The work focuses on linear and random-feature regression and does not explain highly nonlinear underdetermined models. Reported simulation risks are averages over 100 training sets, but the supplied text gives no uncertainty intervals for these results.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible result rows omitted. Cited findings about neural networks and other methods are prior work, not this paper's own results.

untested.parts: No natural-label versus fixed-random-label neural-network comparison.
No trained neural-network width sweep or classification-error comparison beyond the width required for interpolation.
No convolutional versus fully connected network comparison.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD comparison.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurement or comparison with generalization gaps.
No removal of memorized training examples.

record.verdict_notes: The row states indicate that these measures cannot determine the named versions, not that the reported regression effects are absent. The record's V2 support verdict should be removed.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison with natural labels.
Tests linear regression and random Fourier features, not one-hidden-layer ReLU networks on MNIST or downsampled CIFAR-10; does not test widening those specified networks.
No convolutional versus fully connected network comparison.
No adaptive versus SGD optimizer comparison.

rows.subject: spiked covariance model, minimum-norm OLS estimator
rows.operation_detail: Varied predictor dimensionality and measured expected normalized MSE for the minimum-norm OLS estimator.
rows.baseline: OLS expected normalized MSE, which becomes very large near p ≈ n
rows.value: Minimum-norm OLS expected MSE quickly decreased as p increased beyond n.
rows.note: The paper reports the trend in text; the figure shows the sweep. This is linear regression, not the specified ReLU setting.
rows.check: The reported risk decrease is supported, but the subject is a linear estimator, not a toy neural network. Increasing predictor dimensionality does not test V2's network-width effect.

rows.subject: spiked covariance model, ridge estimator
rows.operation_detail: Varied predictor dimensionality and compared the minimum-risk ridge estimator with minimum-norm OLS.
rows.baseline: Minimum-norm OLS; the optimal ridge estimator's risk was close to oracle risk for all dimensionalities.
rows.value: The gain over minimum-norm OLS became smaller as p > n grew and eventually disappeared in the p ≫ n regime.
rows.note: Risk comparison across dimensionalities; not a neural-network width experiment.
rows.check: This compares optimally regularized ridge regression with minimum-norm OLS, rather than measuring neural-network widening. The subject_kind should not be toy_network. The ridge advantage concerns nonnegative penalties; allowing negative penalties improves risk at sufficiently large p.

rows.subject: spiked covariance model, ridge estimator
rows.operation_detail: Measured expected normalized MSE across ridge penalties, including negative values.
rows.measure: Expected normalized MSE as a function of ridge penalty
rows.value: The lowest risk was achieved at λopt = −150.
rows.note: This reports a regularization optimum, not the test-error effect of widening specified ReLU networks.
rows.check: The negative ridge optimum is correctly reported, but measures regularization choice at fixed dimensionality. It bears on no version, and the subject is a linear estimator.

rows.subject: MNIST random Fourier features regression
rows.operation_detail: Measured test-set risk across ridge penalties for regression on digit value using random Fourier features.

conditions.value: Random Fourier features; W elements N(0, σ = 0.1)

rows.baseline: For λ ∈ R+, risk is minimized at λ = 0.
rows.value: For the 80/100 training sets with s²min > 100, risk was minimized at λopt ≈ −80.
rows.note: Random Fourier features are used for regression; this is not the specified ReLU width comparison.
rows.check: Fixed-width random Fourier feature regression on digit values does not test V2. The optimum near −80 describes risk averaged over the selected 80 training sets, not necessarily each training set's optimum.

rows.subject: random-predictor-augmented spiked covariance model, minimum-norm OLS estimator
rows.operation_detail: Added q random predictors with variance λopt/q, fit minimum-norm OLS, and measured risk as q increased.
rows.baseline: At q = 0, the original model's expected MSE
rows.value: As p + q passed n, MSE began to decrease and approached the ridge estimator's limiting value; q ≈ 200 was already close.
rows.note: This is an explicit predictor-augmentation result in a linear model; it does not test the specified ReLU networks.
rows.check: Adding random covariates to linear regression does not measure neural-network widening. The near-limit result at q ≈ 200 refers to the estimator truncated to the original p coefficients; the full augmented estimator converges more slowly. The subject_kind should not be toy_network.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Linear regression under the paper's spiked-covariance simulation
reader_labels.reason: Expected minimum-norm OLS risk falls as predictor dimensionality increases beyond n (R1); adding random predictors also yields decreasing risk after p + q exceeds n (R5). These results support the broad post-interpolation pattern, but not the version's specified ReLU architecture or datasets.
